# 2. Represent a value object as a readonly struct generated by a source generator

Date: 2026-09-14

## Status

Accepted

## Context

A single-value value object — an IBAN, a customer id, a currency amount — needs to be a distinct type in the
domain while remaining its underlying type at every boundary it crosses: JSON, a database column, a
query-string parameter, an OpenAPI schema.

Three representations were available:

- **A `class` wrapper.** Familiar, nullable, easy to write by hand. Costs a reference type's 24-byte header,
  method table pointer and field per instance, and reintroduces null into a domain that had eliminated it.
- **A `record struct`.** Free equality and a `with` expression. But both bypass validation: `with` produces an
  instance that never passed through `Validate`, and compiler-generated field-wise equality ignores any
  configured comparison, so `Comparison = StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase` would silently mean nothing.
- **A `readonly struct` whose members are generated.**

Writing those members by hand is not realistic: a complete value object is roughly 400 lines — constructor,
`Create`/`TryCreate`/`CreateUnchecked`, `Parse`/`TryParse` over both string and span, `ToString`/`TryFormat`,
equality, ordering, a JSON converter, a `TypeConverter`, and runtime registration. Multiplied by every value
object in a domain, and kept consistent as rules change, that is not maintainable.

The one hole in the struct approach is real: a struct can always be brought into existence uninitialized, and
`default(Iban)` would hold a value that never passed validation. A struct cannot close that by itself.

## Decision

We will represent a value object as a `readonly partial struct` marked `[ValueObject<T>]`, with its entire
implementation emitted by a Roslyn incremental generator, and we will close the `default` hole with an analyzer
rather than at run time: `VO0010` makes `default(T)` a compile error, opt-out per type with
`AllowDefault = true`.

Rules are declared once on the attribute and carried by the generator into every place they matter — validation,
the EF Core column, the OpenAPI schema — rather than restated per integration.

The measurements behind the memory claims are in
[Benchmarks](https://adcodicem.github.io/AdCodicem.ValueObjects/benchmarks), including where the struct loses.

## Consequences

Holding 100 000 struct wrappers allocates exactly what holding 100 000 bare strings allocates, to the byte; the
class equivalent costs four times the memory and twice the time. Dictionary lookups and sorts stay
allocation-free because the generated equality, hashing and comparison keep the hot paths generic. Null is gone
from the domain.

What this costs:

- **The struct boxes when it crosses a non-generic boundary.** Hence the split between the typed path
  (`IValueObject<TSelf, TValue>`, used by every generic integration) and the boxed path
  (`ValueObjectDescriptor`, for callers that only know a `Type`). Two paths means a defect can live in one and
  be invisible to tests of the other — which has happened, and is why `DescriptorTests.cs` exists.
- **Consumers depend on a generator, and generators are constrained.** They never observe each other's output,
  which is the entire reason `AdCodicem.ValueObjects.Json` exists as a hand-written factory the System.Text.Json
  generator can see, and why `Pattern` compiles a `Regex` at run time instead of using `[GeneratedRegex]`.
  Emitted code must fully qualify every name, because it cannot rely on the consumer's usings.
- **A compile error can appear in code the consumer cannot edit.** `EmitCompilerGeneratedFiles` and the
  diagnostics are the mitigation; it remains a worse experience than a hand-written type.
- **`AllowDefault = true` is an escape hatch that gives back the guarantee.** It exists because tests and some
  interop genuinely need it, and it is the one way a consumer can hold an unvalidated value.

Reversing this would mean regenerating every consumer's domain types in a different shape, and changing how
their values serialize. It is not practically reversible after 1.0.
